analysis.one_liner: Protects patients from surprise out-of-network medical bills and speeds cheaper generic drugs to market.
analysis.headline: This bipartisan bill, which would have banned surprise medical bills, cleared the Senate health committee in July 2019 and was placed on the Senate calendar, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar hospitals, doctors, and air ambulance operators from sending patients surprise bills for out-of-network care received during emergencies or at in-network facilities, and would pay those providers the median in-network rate instead. It would speed approval of generic and biosimilar drugs by curbing delay tactics like patent-gaming and repetitive citizen petitions, limit what pharmacy benefit managers can charge, ban gag clauses that hide prices, raise the tobacco purchase age to 21, and fund vaccination and public health data programs [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Insured patients who get hit with surprise bills after an ER visit, ambulance ride, or in-network hospital stay; patients who need cheaper generic and biosimilar versions of brand-name drugs; and young adults no longer able to buy tobacco at 18 [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Out-of-network emergency care and ancillary services at in-network facilities would be billed at in-network cost-sharing rates, and providers would be barred from billing patients beyond that amount, with penalties up to $10,000 per violation [S2][S4].
Surprise air ambulance bills would be ended the same way: patient cost-sharing capped at in-network levels and payment set at the median in-network rate [S2][S4].

Generic and biosimilar approvals would be expedited by requiring brand-name makers to disclose their patents, tightening the standard for citizen petitions filed mainly to delay competitors, and closing exclusivity loopholes that keep cheap versions off the market [S2][S4].

Pharmacy benefit managers would face limits on what they can charge insurers and enrollees based on what they pay pharmacies, plus new plan oversight; gag clauses hiding price and quality information from employers would be banned [S2][S4].
The federal tobacco purchase age would rise from 18 to 21 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospital systems and emergency-physician staffing companies that rely on out-of-network billing, air ambulance operators, brand-name drugmakers, and pharmacy benefit managers would lose revenue and negotiating leverage; insurers would have to pay the median in-network rate on disputed bills [S2][S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, air ambulances, brand drugmakers, PBMs

drawbacks.text: Out-of-network providers would be paid a government-set median in-network rate with no arbitration process, an approach hospitals and physician groups publicly argued would let insurers underpay them and could strain emergency-room and rural hospital finances; a rival arbitration approach was pending in the House [S4].

Patients could still be billed out-of-network rates after an emergency admission if, once stabilized, they were given notice, an out-of-network price estimate, and a referral option and then signed a written consent assuming full responsibility for the costs [S4].

The bill targets generic-competition barriers and PBM pricing practices but does not directly cap the list prices of brand-name drugs or premiums, so its effect on total drug and health spending would be gradual rather than immediate [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections are substantial and concrete: surprise bills of thousands of dollars from out-of-network ER doctors and air ambulances are among the most feared medical costs, and this bill would have eliminated most of them. The main cost falls on providers who priced out-of-network care high precisely because patients had no choice, and on brand-name drugmakers whose delay tactics keep cheaper copies off the market. The honest caveats are that the median-rate benchmark was contested by provider groups who preferred arbitration, that a signed-consent loophole remains for post-emergency care, and that the bill leaves underlying list prices and premiums mostly untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee approved it with bipartisan leadership and put it on the Senate calendar in July 2019, but the majority leader never brought it up for a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021 [S6][S1].

narrative.text: Introduced June 19, 2019 by Senator Lamar Alexander (R-TN) together with Senator Patty Murray (D-WA), the chair and ranking member of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and referred to that committee [S1][S4][S6].
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably on June 26, 2019, and it was formally reported on July 8, 2019 with an amendment in the nature of a substitute [S6].
It was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 133) on July 8, 2019 — the last action ever taken on the bill [S6].
No floor vote, motion, or further action occurred in the remaining year and a half of the 116th Congress [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospital systems, emergency-physician staffing companies, air ambulance operators, brand-name drugmakers, and pharmacy benefit managers kept their existing billing and patent practices for another Congress, and insured patients kept facing surprise bills and paying brand-name prices.

for.name: Lamar Alexander
for.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, chaired the committee markup that reported it favorably, and formally reported it to the Senate in July 2019.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.role: Ranking Member, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its co-lead, making it a bipartisan committee effort from the start.

for.name: Two additional senators — one Democrat and one Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total sponsorship to four senators across both parties.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought S. 1895 to the Senate floor for a vote; the bill sat on the calendar for a year and a half while a dispute over how to set out-of-network payments — benchmark rates versus arbitration — went unresolved between the House, the White House, hospitals, and insurers.

against.name: Hospital, physician, and air ambulance lobbying coalition
against.role: Out-of-network providers facing the billing ban
against.what_they_did: Ran a major lobbying campaign against the bill's median in-network rate benchmark, pushing instead for an arbitration process that would let them contest insurer payments — a fight that stalled final action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was co-led by the Republican committee chair and the top committee Democrat and had one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor, but it never reached the floor, so no roll-call ever recorded where the parties stood [S5].

industries.industry: Hospital systems and emergency-physician staffing companies
industries.note: Their business model of sending large out-of-network bills to patients treated at in-network hospitals would be shut down, with payment set at the median in-network rate instead. Patients' gain from protection against surprise bills is these companies' lost revenue.
Air ambulance surprise bills — often tens of thousands of dollars for a single flight — would be capped at in-network cost-sharing with payment at the median in-network rate.

Patent transparency requirements, tighter limits on delay-by-citizen-petition, and closure of exclusivity loopholes would let generic and biosimilar competitors reach patients sooner. Delay tactics that keep prices high are exactly what the bill targets.

The bill limits what PBMs can charge insurers and enrollees relative to what they pay pharmacies and requires health plan oversight of PBM services, cutting into the spread pricing and rebate practices that raise what patients pay at the counter.
Faster approvals, published patent lists, and anti-blocking rules expand their market; cheaper versions of drugs reaching patients is both this industry's gain and the public's.

Insurers would have to pay the median in-network rate on disputed out-of-network claims, but they gain from bans on gag clauses, new tools to oversee PBMs, and requirements to give enrollees real cost estimates. The bill protects their customers without expanding coverage or paying them new subsidies.
